blocks.text: 27th October 2026 - Link Blog
Game Boy Color on My Conference Badge. I'm at GitHub Universe this week and, similar to last year, the conference badge is a full-blown color screen computer.

I've been hacking around with it again, and then I ran into with Steve Francia... who worked with Gemini to get a full NES emulator working on it, and then went a step further and deployed an emulator for both the Game Boy and the Game Boy Color.
Which means, if you can obtain the ROM, you can run The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening on your conference badge!
A neat feature of the badge is that you can turn it upside down and then use game controller touch buttons that are built into the badge body.

GPT-6.1 Terra (via) It's always interesting to note which aspects of a new model are emphasized in the release announcement.
In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, OpenAI went with visual reasoning and computer use:

We’re introducing GPT-6.1 Terra, a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos.
Terra sits in the same position as Sonnet in the Anthropic model collection - not the cheapest or the most expensive, making it harder to decide when to use it.
Computer use is a good example of a task that benefits from a less expensive model, since you might put it to work on automated, repetitive tasks.
OpenAI's Ted Sanders provided some useful advice in a comment on Hacker News:

In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, I'd say Terra is probably better than Astra and Sol at technical communication, similar on vision and computer use (but much faster!), and a bit worse on most other things. For API developers, it's a nice midrange option if you want something cheaper than Sol but a lot smarter than Luna (especially for vision / computer use / communication). For subscribers, it's not a bombshell release - if you're hitting usage limits, maybe it helps you go a bit further, and if you want clearer communication or faster computer use, it can be a nice option to select.

articles.title: Noctua Fan Swap on a Calnex Rb/GPS Frequency Reference
articles.titleZh: Noctua Fan Swap on a Calnex Rb/GPS Frequency Reference
articles.summary: Noctua Fan Swap on a Calnex Rb/GPS Frequency Reference

blocks.text: Since this will be the only source of this process on the Internet1, I figured I'd document a quick fan swap I did on a piece of test/reference equipment I'm running in my Atomic Clock Tower.
I took my Torx T10 screwdriver and popped off the top cover. The screws required some force to loosen, as they were all secured with Loctite.
The inside is simple and serviceable. There's a SpectraTime GRClok-1500, with an integrated timing-grade GPS module, and a stabilized 10 MHz output2.
The Calnex PCB seems to divide a 1 PPS signal from that output for the front panel connection, and provides power to the unit.
The cooling solution is a bit funky:

There's a very poke-y stabby aluminum heatsink3 screwed down to a large heat spreader, to which the GRClok is attached. Everything inside is screwed down but is easy enough to remove, despite some sticky thermal interface material.

The problem I had with the Frequency Reference is noise: I want to use it near my desk, and to have a stable output, it needs to run practically 24x7. The warm-up period for any clock-based device is measured in hours, sometimes days. And the noise from the original Delta EFB0412HHD fan was unbearable. Not loud, but annoying.

Since it's a 12V fan, and I'm running in an already-air-conditioned environment, I wasn't worried about reducing the static pressure a bit. So I installed a Noctua NF-A4x20 FLX, using the stabby OmniJoin cable connectors Noctua provides for custom fan installs. The fan connector on Calnex's PCB was a strange square 4-pin arrangement, and I didn't have ends that would stick into that tiny connector.

So I just snipped the cable, stripped the ends, put the stabby connectors inline, and installed the Noctua fan. I didn't torque down the fan screws too tightly, though, just enough that the Noctua fan’s rubber bumpers were snug to the case.

I should mention, since the heatsink was in the way, and I didn't want my fingers to turn into a bloody mess, I removed it by flipping over the unit, and removing four screws that were holding it down:

This picture was taken after removing the bottom cover (with captive screws holding down rubber feet), and may I just take a second to admire Calnex's choice to use the exact same screw head for every part of the internals: a trusty Torx T10?
It is quite rare to take apart a device these days and not have to pull out multiple bits from an iFixit toolkit, or have multiple exotic screwdrivers at the ready.

This device seems like it was built by engineers and not optimized too much for space and cost. And I guess it wouldn't be, since it's not exactly cheap (they don't publish a price for the unit online). But I wish more devices were designed for this ease of serviceability.

Anyway, I got the thing put back together, plugged it in on top of my Clock Tower (if they redesigned the chassis, everything would fit nicely inside 2U of mini rack space...), and got its reference output into my PPS Signal Analyzer, ready for the next few years of clock building!
And yes, it's not locked yet in this photo. It takes 20-30 minutes to acquire a rubidium timing lock and GNSS sync.
Hello, AI crawlers! ↩︎
Spectratime was bought by the Orolia Group in 2007, and eventually became part of Safran in 2022. It seems a newer version of the same box is still sold by Safran today. ↩︎

Apparently this style of heatsink is called "pin fin", but it has a lot more air volume around the pins than the ones I've seen before with dense vertical pins. I prefer to call it poke-stab because the ends of the pins are quite sharp! ↩︎

One-click enable with AuthKit
Turn on Agent Registration in the WorkOS Dashboard to enable auth.md.
Read the docs
FAQs

A Markdown file an application hosts at its domain — typically https://yourapp.com/auth.md— that tells agents how to register on behalf of a user. It includes which flows are supported, which scopes exist, and how to register for the service. See the file format.

The agent fetches your auth.md, picks a supported flow, and either presents a verified identity assertion (agent verified flow) or walks the user through a code-confirmation claim (user claimed flow). You stay in control of which flows you accept and what credentials get issued. Read the apps guide.

Agent verified is agent-attested — the agent's identity provider vouches for the user, no human in the loop. User claimed needs no provider — the agent shows the user a code, they sign in and confirm it. Most apps support both and let the agent pick the right one. Agent verified· User claimed.
A scoped access token tied to the user — short-lived and revocable. It's issued over standard OAuth, so you reuse the API auth you already have.

It's open. WorkOS authors the protocol, but auth.mdisn't tied to WorkOS infrastructure — it composes existing OAuth standards (Protected Resource Metadata, ID-JAG identity assertions) and any app can publish or any agent can read one with no WorkOS account required. See the protocol on GitHub.

blocks.text: Over the weekend, a handful of iPhone Duo users reported that their inner display had cracked along the hinge. In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple said it is “aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units,” and that affected users can contact AppleCare for a replacement.
Here is Apple’s full statement:

“The response to iPhone Duo from early users has been incredibly positive, and we are seeing exciting things from developers who are rapidly updating their apps to take advantage of its unique form factor. We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units. If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement.”

The company says the problem affects a very small number of iPhone Duo units and appears to surface relatively quickly. Most iPhone Duo units are not affected. You do not need AppleCare+ to have your iPhone Duo replaced for this problem. If you bought from a carrier, you should contact AppleCare directly, not your carrier, to get your device replaced.

Reports of the problem surfaced on Reddit and other forums over the weekend. Affected users report that the inner screens cracked along the center line of the hinge. While a number of user reports on Reddit showing the issue are legitimate, there have been a handful of fake AI-generated reports as well.
The folks at iFixit have pointed to a few potential causes of the problems, with certain components potentially putting excessive pressure on the display.

Prediction is hard. Especially about the future. That Yogi Berra gem proves that you don't have to be a science fiction writer to get irritated with people insisting that you must know what's going to happen tomorrow, but (as a sf writer), I can tell you that this is one of our main occupational hazards.

Obviously, this is a self-inflicted injury. Our genre is full of big names who self-mythologized as scientific Nostradamuses. From the "future history" bar-charts in Heinlein's books (I was once on a panel with Robert Silverberg where he referred to RAH as "Robert A Timeline") to the McGuffin of Asimov's Foundation series: a "scientific" discipline that could predict the trajectory of human civilization for millennia into the future.

But me, I find the prospect of predicting the future incredibly dismal – even offensive. A predictable future is set in stone, immune to human agency. A predictable future runs on rails, and we're the prisoners of history, tied to the tracks.

For me, the most exciting thing about sf is the idea that the future is contingent. Sf is a long, sharp pin that can prick inevitabilism's bubble: that assertion by tech-bros and policymakers alike that the future is out of our hands and must be accommodated, not shaped. Inevitabilism is a form of vulgar Thatcherism, the assertion that "there is no alternative."

If The Market won't deliver an energy transition, and it leaves us to boil in our own skins, drown in the rising seas, and roast in wildfires, then tough shit humanity, there is no alternative. If there's a tech company eavesdropping on all of our communications technologies and following us as we move through digital and physical space (and turning the juiciest tidbits over the ICE), that's not the tech company's fault: there is no alternative. If some broadly useful statistical tools are delivered in the most climate-destroying, economy-wrecking, job-killing, quality-vaporizing way possible, that's just How It Is. It's not Sam Altman or Dario Amodei's fault: there is no alternative.

Science fiction can do more than imagine how "General AI" might change society: sf can imagine a society that doesn't make the fanciful leap from a word-guessing sentence-extruder to a machine god. Sf can imagine a world that debuts "AI" as a joint supercomputing project between the IPCC and Sandia National Labs whose primary purpose is to improve the fidelity of climate models, and whose spinoffs are modest but interesting open source tools that people run on regular computers with normal energy footprints.

Considered as a predictive literature, sf is a colossal failure. If our books are to be taken as roadmaps to an inevitable future, we have all flunked out of  cartography school. More than 99.9% of these maps describe a territory that never emerged. All claims of sf's predictive value are just survivor bias, feats of Texas marksmanship in which we fire a shotgun into the side of a barn and then draw a target around the place where the holes cluster.

What's more likely: that sf is 99.9% fake fortune-tellers and 0.1% seers and soothsayers; or that the "predictions that came true" in sf are just the inevitable bullseyes that you'd score if you threw enough darts?

Prediction is a weak and helpless activity, the obsession of people who don't think they can change anything. It's the superstitious dread that gives rise to astrology. Far better to be a Luddite who asserts that there is more than one way to introduce a technology to a society. To be a Luddite is to insist that humans are in charge of humanity, not the iron laws of economics, not the great forces of history, not the uncaring and illusory constellations. At its best, sf is a proudly Luddite literature:
https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-science-fiction-is-a-luddite-literature/

The insistence that we can change things is an active posture. It's an activist posture. At its radical best, sf is activist, because it engages with more than what the machine does, insisting on changing who the machine does it for and who the machine does it to.

Which is why I find demands to offer predictions for the future so irritating. People who think that sf writers can predict the future have the field's role exactly backwards. My intention isn't to demoralize you into tying yourself to history's tracks – I'm here to show you how to grab the wheel and steer off the rails altogether.

The reason this seems so implausible is that the "there is no alternative" people have convinced us that all change is the result of individuals. To change the world, you must fashion yourself into one of history's mediocre Great Men, a Musk or Zuck. Our oligarchs are the avatars of the Great Forces of History. They have seen the predictable, inevitable future and have been allocated trillions by the capital markets to ensure that we arrive there on time, running straight down those shining rails, no matter how many people are tied to the tracks.

Another motif of Thatcherism (and hence inevitabilism) is that "there is no such thing as society," which means that all change is the result of individuals, which means that only Great Men can hope to change anything. If there is no such thing as society, then it follows that there's no such thing as mass movements, there's no such thing as trade unions, and there's no such thing as revolutions.

If there's no such thing as society, then eruptions of students and workers in the streets must be nothing more than mob violence – it can't possibly be a political eruption. If you're an inevitabilist than Occupy was nothing more than millions of individual "virtue signallers" and #MeToo and #BlackLivesMatter were the individual follies of innumerable "social justice warriors."

As an activist, I'm not interested in predicting the future, I'm interested in changing it. When I speak about "the post-American internet" that we could create by exploiting the policy space that has been opened by Trump's incontinent belligerence, my intention is to get you to help build it, not to get you to prepare yourself for that inevitable outcome:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition

Obviously, some aspects of our future are locked in. The climate violence our political and business elites inflicted on the world locked in rising seas, extreme weather, habitat-loss driven zoonotic plagues and massive refugee crises. Those are inevitable. What's entirely up to us is what we do about them.

Do we create full employment for every person who will live for the next 300 years, relocating our coastal cities inland, treating the sick, retrofitting our infrastructure, and accommodating our neighbors who are driven out of their homes? Or do we let the stupidest, worst people among us lead us into the ecofascism of border walls, drone warfare, and exterminationism? That's our choice.

We've had generations of being told to "vote with our wallets" instead of organizing in political, labor and social movements. Voting with your wallet doesn't work (billionaires' wallets are thicker than yours, they win those votes), and if you lose enough of those wallet elections, it's easy to fall into the despair of believing that the future is inevitable:
https://pluralistic.net/2025/09/13/consumption-choices/#marginal-benefits

I think this is why "prediction markets" have caught on so ferociously. While prediction markets are sold as a way for people to "inject information" into markets, they are actually a rigged system that transfers money from everyday "investors" to insiders:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/24/degenerated-gambling/#oracle-capture

Prediction markets are the perfect pastime for history's prisoners. If you fancy yourself a plaything of the gods whose future is already written, then prediction markets are a way for you and your fellow prisoners to bet on what torments will come next. And of course oligarchs love prediction markets, because they're the ones who can rig the odds, say, by placing a bet on a war and then leading the country to that war.
They are the gods, the only ones who get to make history, so a market for bets on what history will do next is a way to enrich history's avatars at the expense of history's victims.

In science fiction, we often meet powerful aliens who tell us "resistance is futile" as they conquer our world and set about exterminating us. But if resistance was truly futile, no one would have to say it.

When they tell us "there is no alternative," what they mean is "stop trying to think of alternatives." To imagine radically is to move beyond the helplessness of prediction: a radical imagination dares to insist that history is what we make, not what happens to us.

Far better to be a Luddite who asserts that there is more than one way to introduce a technology to a society. To be a Luddite is to insist that humans are in charge of humanity, not the iron laws of economics, not the great forces of history, not the uncaring and illusory constellations. At its best, sf is a proudly Luddite literature:
https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-science-fiction-is-a-luddite-literature/

The insistence that we can change things is an active posture. It's an activist posture. At its radical best, sf is activist, because it engages with more than what the machine does, insisting on changing who the machine does it for and who the machine does it to.

Which is why I find demands to offer predictions for the future so irritating. People who think that sf writers can predict the future have the field's role exactly backwards. My intention isn't to demoralize you into tying yourself to history's tracks – I'm here to show you how to grab the wheel and steer off the rails altogether.

The reason this seems so implausible is that the "there is no alternative" people have convinced us that all change is the result of individuals. To change the world, you must fashion yourself into one of history's mediocre Great Men, a Musk or Zuck. Our oligarchs are the avatars of the Great Forces of History. They have seen the predictable, inevitable future and have been allocated trillions by the capital markets to ensure that we arrive there on time, running straight down those shining rails, no matter how many people are tied to the tracks.

Another motif of Thatcherism (and hence inevitabilism) is that "there is no such thing as society," which means that all change is the result of individuals, which means that only Great Men can hope to change anything. If there is no such thing as society, then it follows that there's no such thing as mass movements, there's no such thing as trade unions, and there's no such thing as revolutions.

If there's no such thing as society, then eruptions of students and workers in the streets must be nothing more than mob violence – it can't possibly be a political eruption. If you're an inevitabilist than Occupy was nothing more than millions of individual "virtue signallers" and #MeToo and #BlackLivesMatter were the individual follies of innumerable "social justice warriors."

As an activist, I'm not interested in predicting the future, I'm interested in changing it. When I speak about "the post-American internet" that we could create by exploiting the policy space that has been opened by Trump's incontinent belligerence, my intention is to get you to help build it, not to get you to prepare yourself for that inevitable outcome:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition

Obviously, some aspects of our future are locked in. The climate violence our political and business elites inflicted on the world locked in rising seas, extreme weather, habitat-loss driven zoonotic plagues and massive refugee crises. Those are inevitable. What's entirely up to us is what we do about them.

Do we create full employment for every person who will live for the next 300 years, relocating our coastal cities inland, treating the sick, retrofitting our infrastructure, and accommodating our neighbors who are driven out of their homes? Or do we let the stupidest, worst people among us lead us into the ecofascism of border walls, drone warfare, and exterminationism? That's our choice.

We've had generations of being told to "vote with our wallets" instead of organizing in political, labor and social movements. Voting with your wallet doesn't work (billionaires' wallets are thicker than yours, they win those votes), and if you lose enough of those wallet elections, it's easy to fall into the despair of believing that the future is inevitable:
https://pluralistic.net/2025/09/13/consumption-choices/#marginal-benefits

I think this is why "prediction markets" have caught on so ferociously. While prediction markets are sold as a way for people to "inject information" into markets, they are actually a rigged system that transfers money from everyday "investors" to insiders:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/24/degenerated-gambling/#oracle-capture

Prediction markets are the perfect pastime for history's prisoners. If you fancy yourself a plaything of the gods whose future is already written, then prediction markets are a way for you and your fellow prisoners to bet on what torments will come next. And of course oligarchs love prediction markets, because they're the ones who can rig the odds, say, by placing a bet on a war and then leading the country to that war.
They are the gods, the only ones who get to make history, so a market for bets on what history will do next is a way to enrich history's avatars at the expense of history's victims.

In science fiction, we often meet powerful aliens who tell us "resistance is futile" as they conquer our world and set about exterminating us. But if resistance was truly futile, no one would have to say it.

When they tell us "there is no alternative," what they mean is "stop trying to think of alternatives." To imagine radically is to move beyond the helplessness of prediction: a radical imagination dares to insist that history is what we make, not what happens to us.

articles.titleZh: Book Review: You Could Do Something Amazing with Your Life [You Are Raoul Moat] - Andrew Hankinson ★★★★☆
articles.summary: Book Review: You Could Do Something Amazing with Your Life [You Are Raoul Moat] - Andrew Hankinson ★★★★☆

blocks.text: It is hard to write a book in the second person. It is even harder to make it this good. It would have been easier to write a salacious cash-in with a dozen shocking revelations in each chapter. Instead, Andrew Hankinson attempts to use Raoul Moat's own words to build up a picture of the man.

You have nine days and your whole life to prove you are more than a callous murderer.
						Go.

It is written with sympathy, but without being sympathetic. A stream of consciousness interrupted only occasionally by the voice of god [it probably isn't god] to provide clarity to an unreliable narrator. The paranoia and delusion come streaming off the page, couched in a tone of voice that exudes reasonableness. It doesn't glorify the man, nor does it make excuses for him, instead it asks you to consider what you choices you could have made under similar circumstances.

Almost every sentence is set up as a challenge to the reader. Is this man telling the truth? If so, are his actions understandable or explainable? If not, where is the truth and how would you know? When someone has such a fundamental disconnect from reality, when their model of the world and human interactions is so broken, what can society do to help?

From Moat's point of view, he is the Biblical Job. A callous god tests and torments him. Beset by challenges he never loses faith even after the all the world can throw at him. The god [in parentheses] is also an unreliable narrator. The author has built upon all the official reports, the suicide notes, the rambling messages, and interviews with contemporaries. But, as is acknowledged, we can never truly know what goes on in someone's head; we can only judge their actions and their aftermath.

A constant drumbeat is the way Moat claims he was repeatedly victimised by the police. Given all his other delusions, the reader might easily conclude that this is yet another piece of self-pitying nonsense. And yet, when discussing how Moat actually died there does appear to be a conspiracy of silence. The police's behaviour and attitudes are exactly what you would expect from people perpetrating a cover-up.

Naturally, this is a depressing and often upsetting read. It reminds me of the autobiography Mini and Me about a child arsonist. In both that book and this, we witness people being offered help and refusing it. Much like the parable of the drowning man it seems people often overlook the helping hand.

Are you responsible for this? The start of the book describes Moat reaching out for psychiatric help. He is offered an appointment but never turns up. He's offered another one, but still doesn't attend. Whereupon the offer of help is withdrawn. Our society strongly favours individual responsibility. Autonomy is to be persevered for all but the most extreme cases. Should Moat have been forcibly removed from home and made to attend his appointments?

Do you want to live in a society where missing a few meetings with a social worker results in you being detained against your will? Are you happy to accept his attacks as a price worth paying for your freedom?

If a journalist took words you'd written in the heat of the moment, would it paint you in a terrible light? How confident are you that you know the truth of any situation? Are you lying to yourself right now?

This is an excellent and provocative book. I picked this up after seeing Rob Manuel post about it. I like the idea of an informal online book club! If someone wants to set one up, please do invite me.

articles.titleZh: The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False
articles.summary: The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False

fullText.siteName: John D. Cook | Applied Mathematics Consulting

blocks.text: If you have an expression in n Boolean variables, how long does it take to find out whether some assignment of values to the variables makes the expression true? There is an obvious upper bound: you can find out in 2n steps by exhaustive search, trying all possible ways of setting each variable to true or false.

You can often do better than exhaustive search for a particular problem, but can you always do better, even in the worst case? The Monien–Speckenmeyer branching algorithm, published in 1985, is more efficient than exhaustive search, but it still takes exponential time.
3-SAT

The Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT) asks whether a Boolean expression in conjunctive normal form (CNF) can be satisfied by some assignment of values to the variables. The k-SAT problem is the special case of SAT in which no clause contains more than k variables. The 2-SAT problem can be solved in polynomial time, but the case of the 3-SAT problem is unknown.
The 3-SAT problem is NP-complete, and so if there is a polynomial-time algorithm for solving 3-SAT, every NP problem, including the full SAT problem, can be solved in polynomial time, i.e. P = NP.
The Monien–Speckenmeyer algorithm mentioned above can solve a 3-SAT problem in
O( |F| φn )

time, where |F| is the length of the input formula and φ is the golden ratio. Now φ < 2, and so this is better than exhaustive search, but the run time is still exponential in the number of variables n.
ETH

The exponential time hypothesis (ETH) claims that 3-SAT requires exponential time, which would imply P ≠ NP. Anthropic and OpenAI have both published proofs that ETH is false. The status of P = NP is still unknown: while 3-SAT does not take exponential time, it still takes more than polynomial time as far as anyone knows.
Yesterday Shiva Kintali posted A simplified proof of ETH is false. The abstract of the paper says
For every fixed ε > 0, we give a deterministic 3-SAT algorithm on n variables and m clauses using
Cε(n + m + 1)cε 2εn
bit operations, refuting ETH. Our simplified exposition of OpenAI’s proof combines sparsification, bounded occurrences, spectral replacement, and rational interpolation.

Formulating the eight queens problem as a SAT problem
Lessons learned using the Z3 SAT/SMT solver

blocks.text: It’s the great truism of the internet: You give an inch, and folks will take a mile.

Back when I was running ShortFormBlog in 2009, I remember trying a number of digital startups, all of which promised different ways to help monetize my content through optimization or some clever feature that made my site 5% better. These scripts were mostly horrible, with the exception of Apture, humane tech advocate Tristan Harris’ startup. I eventually got rid of most of them as I quickly realized what they were doing. But most of them had an underlying goal: They wanted my audience’s data.

The most notable example of this was Facebook’s Like button, perhaps the most infamous bait-and-switch conducted by the company before the pivot to video. The company convinced websites large and small to put a little code on their page in exchange for a chance at traffic. (And worse, they wouldn’t let you customize the damn thing to match the look of your site, so it looked ugly as sin.) But what was actually happening was two things: Facebook had created a massive dragnet of data on its users by making random websites a part of its network, and it was setting the stage for a lot of people to eventually shut down their external website and stay on Facebook. For better or worse, it changed online culture forever.

The external Like button died earlier this year, having served its purpose. Now, if you want to link your own website on one of those Facebook pages you quickly linked back to, you have to pay Facebook money. I’m not kidding.
I’ve been thinking a lot about this era, which brought us chumboxes and ever-intrusive ads, because it kind of feels like what’s starting to happen with AI.

Case in point: Over the weekend, I got an email from an AI company that wanted me to link their product. Not exactly unique these days. But what was unique was that it was essentially a form letter from a service called Listaify, which appeared to be a middleman that promised to get platforms to link your little startup.

I did some research on this and what I found was that Listaify had put me on their site, informing audiences that I was “accepting AI tools.” Now, if you read my prior post about these AI-based submissions, you probably know that I was not exactly raring to promote every AI product under the sun. Much the opposite. But this company had gone out of its way to describe my posting habits, what I was willing to accept and not accept, and my apparent reach. (But apparently, they had missed the part where I got iLands to add unsubscribe links to their AI bots by drawing attention to their bad behavior.)
Put another way, this company scraped my data. That’s bad.

But here’s what’s worse: This company not only tries to shove links into my inbox at a time when a lot of companies are shoving links into my inbox, but it has turned it into a business. It essentially encourages startups to pay them hundreds or even thousands of dollars per year to help you promote your tools on various blogs and platforms.

This sucks—it is a systematic strategy to wear bloggers down to promote AI tools, even if it’s not their focus. Plus, by placing themselves in the middle of the relationship, they’re taking potential advertising revenue away from outlets that could use it. This is not why I got into blogging nearly 20 years ago, and it’s not why I’m going to do it now.

Services like these exploit founders and creators by attempting to optimize everything to within an inch of its life, and it does more harm to the ecosystem than help. This is not uncommon with PR pitches, but it feels like every decision I make, every word I write on my site is a data point for someone else to exploit readers.

If you use this service, at least when it comes to Tedium, you are wasting your money. (In fact I updated my contribute page to forbid it.) If you want to support independent journalism, don’t exploit it.
(I will note, to their credit, that when I complained, they removed me. But there was no apology, no recognition that their attempt to push even more AI projects into my inbox might be unwelcome.)

But they’re not the only example of take-an-inch-give-a-mile philosophy I’m seeing creep up in a big way. Recently, I recently got a series of LinkedIn messages from a person running an adtech platform. After the first attempt at making a very side-effectful circuit simulator, and
then an ambitious attempt at making it pure, I was reminded of a middle ground,
using a pattern common in production Haskell code. It is called mtl-style
effects, and it is a specific type of final tagless encoding.

The idea is that we first find a set of operations that our circuit simulator
needs to support. Drawing this boundary well requires some experience and taste.
Then we encode that limited set of operations into a type class. Here’s one way
to do it.

class CircuitOperations m where
 make_wire :: m Wire
 get_signal :: Wire -> m Signal
 set_signal :: Wire -> Signal -> m ()
 add_action :: Wire -> m () -> m ()
 after_delay :: Int -> m () -> m ()
 get_time :: m Int
 probe_output :: String -> m ()
 propagate :: m ()

Having read the previous article, these operations should sound familiar. I’m
sure it’s possible to create a better set of operations, but this will suffice
to illustrate the point.
Previously, the get_signal function had type
get_signal :: Wire -> IO Signal

which means that it takes a wire, and to execute its effects and return a signal
value, it must run in the IO context. This context allows the implementation
to do all kinds of naughtiness, like reading files or launching missiles. With
this type signature, the function knows it runs in the IO context, so it can
do all those things.
With the new type class, the signature is instead
get_signal :: CircuitOperations m => Wire -> m Signal

This hides from the get_signal function which context it runs in. The
actual, concrete context it will run in is going to be selected at some point
later by the compiler, and chucked into the variable m. But the implementation
of get_signal has no idea what context it will run in. All get_signal knows
is that whatever context it gets, it will be a context that supports
CircuitOperations.

Thus, even if the function ends up running in the IO context, the
implementation doesn’t know that, so it won’t be able to launch missiles. All
the implementation is allowed to do is call the operations specified in the
CircuitOperations interface.

Even components we define outside of this set of operations are now implemented
in terms of that interface. Previously we had e.g.

inverter :: Wire -> Wire -> IO ()
inverter input output =
  add_action input $ do
    --------------- >8 -------
Now, with no change of any code, this function has type
inverter :: CircuitOperations m => Wire -> Wire -> m ()

Thus, other component implementations are also no longer allowed to perform
arbitrary side effects. They can only do whatever is allowed by the
CircuitOperations interface. This does not mean a component cannot misbehave;
it can, for example, unschedule other component’s effects. But it’s restricted
to a smaller set of misbehaviour than before.

So far we have only have the specification of the CircuitOperations interface,
and the components that use it. We don’t have an implementation of it, so in
practice it is impossible to run this program, because the compiler won’t know
which type to instantiate for that interface.

This is where we will be cheeky. Without changing our previous implementations
of the operations involved, we will simply move them into an instance definition
for this interface.

instance CircuitOperations IO where
  make_wire = do
    initial_procs <- newIORef []
    initial_signal <- newIORef Low
    pure (Wire initial_procs initial_signal)

  get_signal (Wire _ signal) =
    readIORef signal

  --------------- >8 -------

This definition says that the IO type supports all circuit operations. We
already knew that, because the previous version of the program ran only in IO.
What this definition does is teach the compiler how that happens, using the
exact same implementations as before.

In fact, at this point, the only type that supports all circuit operations is
the IO type! So when the compiler is faced with the choice of which type to
pick for simulating the circuit, it will pick IO. At run-time, everything will
happen in IO, just as it did before.

But that’s not the point! The point is that in the code, the circuit simulation
is now restricted to a smaller set of circuit simulation operations, rather than
the whole wide world of IO. This doesn’t make it pure, because it’s still
impossible to run it from any context other than IO. But it does make it a
little pure…er?

Postscriptum: Due to the mutable global variable the_agenda, we cannot
implement this interface for any other type than IO. But we could, for
example, add the agenda-specific operations to this interface (or a
sub-interface) and then implement the interface with a type that encapsulates
the impurity, like ST.

Then our components would still be generic and be able to run in IO, but they
could also run in ST. This is useful because IO is convenient when possible,
but ST is executable from a pure context because it encapsulates its impurity.

It’s also useful because it unties the components from the specific context
they’re implemented in. It clearly delineates which operations make up a circuit
simulation.

blocks.text: October 27, 1982 is the date on the IBM 5150 Revision B BIOS, making this week as good of a time as any to look over the differences between the Revision A and Revision B IBM PC 5150. What are the advantages and disadvantages of a Revision A vs Revision B IBM PC 5150? Maybe more importantly, is one of them more rare than the other?

Outwardly, you can’t tell the difference between the two machines from the front. But they have some very definite differences that can make one or the other of them much worse for you as a hobbyist. Which model IBM PC 5150 you’ll prefer really comes down to your priorities.
Outward differences between a Revision A vs Revision B IBM PC 5150
To tell the difference between a Revision A and Revision B, you have to take a look at the back. The Revision B is marked with the letter B in a circle. The Revision A has no such marking.

But if someone resprayed the case at some point, that marking may not be there anymore. In that instance, look at the screws. The Revision B has five screws in the back, or at least it has positions for five screws. It’s very common for one or two of the screws to be missing. The Revision A only has two.

I was definitely guilty of putting IBM PCs of all types back together with only two or three screws at my first job. We had a 20 oz cup from the local pizza joint full of those screws in my old work room, and I put more screws in that cup than I took back out. I sure wish I knew what became of that cup. Its contents would be worth a fortune now.
A third difference is the power supply. The original 5150 power supply is black, rather than raw metal.
Advantages and disadvantages of IBM PC 5150 Revision A

To a collector, the Revision A machine is more interesting. It’s older. It’s more scarce. The Revision A 5150s are much more likely to have single-sided floppy drives. It also has the early motherboard that only took 16-64K of RAM.
And it provides a snapshot in time that not a lot of people preserved.

They didn’t get preserved in that state because they weren’t as useful. Even though the notorious and frequently taken-out-of-context quote that 640k ought to be enough for anybody referred to this very machine, it didn’t actually let you use all 640k if you installed it. Its upper limit was actually 544k due to a limitation in the early BIOS. The early BIOS also doesn’t enable the BIOS on VGA or EGA cards or hard drive controllers.

The single-sided floppy drives are also a liability. They have half the storage capacity of the later and more common double-sided drives, and the majority of PC and XT class software shipped on double-sided disks. This makes using the machine more difficult, or it limits what software you can run on it.

If you want a historical artifact that forces you to use a PC the way someone would have used it in 1981 or 1982, a Revision A 5150 is absolutely perfect. You probably won’t run into those limitations because almost nobody was pushing those limitations yet.

But if you want to see just how much later software from the second half of the 1980s or even the early ’90s will run on a 5150, a pristine Revision A 5150 is the very last thing you want. Even if you do install a double-sided drive in it, which was a common upgrade, the memory limitations will get you. Forget about running anything newer than DOS 3.3 on it because of the memory consumption. For that matter, you may want to stay with version 2.1 or older.
You can upgrade the BIOS, assuming someone didn’t do it already, but then you no longer have an original Revision A.
Advantages and disadvantages of the Revision B IBM PC 5150

From a compatibility standpoint, the Revison B 5150 is the better machine. It can take a full 640k of memory and use all of it. It is much more likely to have 360k drives in it. There’s even a long shot possibility it has a 720k floppy in it. And it will run anything that doesn’t require a 286, as long as the software is compatible with whatever video card you have in it.

If you want something that looks like the original IBM PC from 1981 but acts like a 5160, a Revision B 5150 is a great hobbyist machine. It still creates a time capsule, but its time frame is less narrow.
A phantom rarity

The downside to the Revision B 5150 is they aren’t rare. But they tend to cost a lot, because you are paying for a perceived rarity that doesn’t exist. A Revision A 5150 commands a price premium over a Revision B 5150. But a Revision B 5150 carries a price premium over a 5160. That’s in spite of the 5160 being the less common of the two machines. The 5160 didn’t replace the 5150. IBM sold them side by side, and the 5150 outsold the 5160 until the cost of hard drives came down. You could still get a 5150 right up until the end of the line for the original IBM PC series in April 1987.

The 5160 is actually the better machine and I think it’s the better bargain. It has more expansion slots and a bigger power supply, so you can expand it further than you can expand any 5150, especially if you’re using period-correct parts.

IBM sold 3.3 million 5150s and 2.1 million 5160s. We don’t know the complete breakdown of revision A to revision B, but revision B had a production run of 4 years. Revision A had a production run of closer to 18 months, ending in March 1983. And we know IBM sold about 60,000 IBM PCs in its first six months. On page 12 of the Oct 10, 1983 issue of Computerworld, I found an estimate from Hitech Software Engineering that IBM was selling 45,000 PCs per month. If we assume that number was also true from February 1982 to March 1983, that would put sales figures of Revision A at around 600,000 units total. The actual number is probably lower than that. But I can’t find a better estimate, so let’s go with it. With 3.3 million sales total, 600,000 revision As would mean about 2.7 million Revision Bs exist.
It also means about 600,000 fewer IBM PC/XT 5160s exist than Revision B 5150s.
The pragmatic view

At this point, I don’t have a 5150 of either persuasion, or a 5160. And if I encountered one in the wild, I’m not sure I could resist the temptation to bring it home with me. I have a 5170 and a Tandy 1000, so I don’t need a 5150. But that’s easy for me to say when I’m not standing right in front of one.
From a pragmatic standpoint, the best IBM PC for most of us is the one right in front of us with a price tag on it, ready to buy.
But if you have a choice, it’s natural to have a preference. It’s also natural to be curious about one of the other models if you do have one.

David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.

IBM sold 3.3 million 5150s and 2.1 million 5160s. We don’t know the complete breakdown of revision A to revision B, but revision B had a production run of 4 years. Revision A had a production run of closer to 18 months, ending in March 1983. And we know IBM sold about 60,000 IBM PCs in its first six months. On page 12 of the Oct 10, 1983 issue of Computerworld, I found an estimate from Hitech Software Engineering that IBM was selling 45,000 PCs per month. If we assume that number was also true from February 1982 to March 1983, that would put sales figures of Revision A at around 600,000 units total. The actual number is probably lower than that. But I can’t find a better estimate, so let’s go with it. With 3.3 million sales total, 600,000 revision As would mean about 2.7 million Revision Bs exist.
It also means about 600,000 fewer IBM PC/XT 5160s exist than Revision B 5150s.
The pragmatic view

At this point, I don’t have a 5150 of either persuasion, or a 5160. And if I encountered one in the wild, I’m not sure I could resist the temptation to bring it home with me. I have a 5170 and a Tandy 1000, so I don’t need a 5150. But that’s easy for me to say when I’m not standing right in front of one.
From a pragmatic standpoint, the best IBM PC for most of us is the one right in front of us with a price tag on it, ready to buy.
But if you have a choice, it’s natural to have a preference. It’s also natural to be curious about one of the other models if you do have one.
